target.title: Simple is as simple does: Plantinga and Ghazālī on divine simplicity
target.thesis: Most of the arguments against divine simplicity credited to Plantinga were nearly perfectly anticipated by al-Ghazālī, and his responses to Avicenna's stronger form of simplicity contain new arguments that remain valuable today.

argument.title: God cannot be a composite

atoms.A: God is a composite of more basic features
atoms.D: God is causally dependent on his distinct properties
atoms.E: God depends on properties such as power, wisdom, and blessedness as final causes
atoms.F: God is simple (not a composite of more basic features)

argument.missing_premise: God is not causally dependent on his distinct properties, either efficiently or as final causes. [~D & ~E]

W4229080938.c001.text: Divine simplicity is the claim that God is not a composite of more basic features.
W4229080938.c001.quote: the notion of divine simplicity, the idea that God is not a composite of more basic features

W4229080938.c002.text: Traditional theists hold that God’s nature is absolutely simple, identical with God, so any dependence on the nature is merely self‑dependence.
W4229080938.c002.quote: God does have a nature, but that nature is absolutely simple – the property of being God, if you will – and so, the divine nature is not a composite of disparate properties out of God’s control. Moreover, God is identical with that nature, and so while God is dependent upon his nature, the dependence is an innocuous case of self‑dependence.

W4229080938.c003.text: Divine simplicity conflicts with the fact that God possesses several properties such as knowledge, power, and will.
W4229080938.c003.quote: divine simplicity flies in the face of the fact that God has several properties, such as knowledge, power, will

W4229080938.c004.text: If God is identical with a single property, then God is a property rather than a person, which is absurd.
W4229080938.c004.quote: if God is identical with that property, God is a property, not a person, which seems absurd

W4229080938.c005.text: Al‑Ghazālī’s critique of divine simplicity anticipates and exceeds Plantinga’s own criticism.
W4229080938.c005.quote: the renowned Muslim theologian Abū Ḥāmid al‑Ghazālī (d. 1111) subjects the philosophical doctrine of simplicity and the grounds for accepting it to a scathing critique, which interestingly anticipates and goes beyond Plantinga’s own critique

W4229080938.c006.text: Avicenna’s stronger version of divine simplicity can answer some of Plantinga’s objections.
W4229080938.c006.quote: Avicenna’s stronger version of divine simplicity can respond to some of Plantinga’s objections

W4229080938.c007.text: Avicenna assumes that if God had distinct properties, those properties would be parts of a whole.
W4229080938.c007.quote: the first assumption is that if God were to have distinct properties, these properties would stand to God as parts to a whole

W4229080938.c008.text: Avicenna assumes that parts taken individually differ from the whole taken collectively.
W4229080938.c008.quote: Avicenna’s second mereological assumption is that parts (or at least proper parts) taken individually are other than or different from the whole taken collectively

W4229080938.c009.text: It is contradictory for something to exist both through itself and through another.
W4229080938.c009.quote: It is simply a contradiction for something to exist both through itself and through another; it is tantamount to saying that something’s existence depends on nothing and depends on something

W4229080938.c010.text: Therefore, the Necessary Existent (God) cannot be a composite; consequently, God’s existence is simple.
W4229080938.c010.quote: Therefore, the Necessary Existent through itself, that is, God, cannot be a composite and if he is not a composite yet he exists, God’s existence is simple

W4229080938.c011.text: Traditional theists fear that a composite God would be causally dependent on his distinct properties.
W4229080938.c011.quote: for traditional theists it is fundamentally the fear that a composite God, that is, a God having distinct properties, attributes, or the like, is in some way causally dependent upon those properties

W4229080938.c012.text: If God were not simple, he would depend on properties like power, wisdom, and blessedness as final causes.
W4229080938.c012.quote: if God were not simple, he would depend upon properties like power, wisdom, blessedness, in the order of final causation

W4229080938.c013.text: Plantinga argues that God possesses accidental properties that correspond to Avicennan relational properties.
W4229080938.c013.quote: Plantinga begins by first arguing that God has accidental properties, which seem to correspond to Avicennan relational properties.

W4229080938.c014.text: Avicenna holds that relational properties do not threaten divine simplicity, while Plantinga maintains that they do.
W4229080938.c014.quote: Avicenna believes that relational properties do not threaten divine simplicity, whereas Plantinga thinks that they do.

W4229080938.c015.text: Avicenna claims relational properties are not genuine properties in the sense of constitutive features.
W4229080938.c015.quote: For Avicenna, purportedly relational properties are not really properties at all, at least not in the sense of constitutive features.

W4229080938.c016.text: Plantinga asserts that possessing a given characterization makes God different from what He would have been without it.
W4229080938.c016.quote: Moreover, maintains Plantinga, possessing a given characterization does make God ‘different from what he would have been had it not characterized him’.

W4229080938.c017.text: Medieval philosophers agree that God’s many actions can be traced to Him, but these effects need not arise from distinct essential properties or characterizations.
W4229080938.c017.quote: Both sides in the medieval debate agreed that God’s ultimately numerous different actions or effects can be traced back to God; however, they also insisted that those different effects of his action need not emanate from different essential properties or even necessarily from different ways of characterizing God.

W4229080938.c018.text: The shift from properties to characteristics does not indicate real differences within the divinity.
W4229080938.c018.quote: Thus, Plantinga’s shift from properties to characteristics need not show that there are real differences within the divinity.

W4229080938.c019.text: Avicenna argues that God’s knowledge of a thing is the ultimate cause of that thing’s existence, so knowing and creating are identical in God.
W4229080938.c019.quote: Avicenna anticipates Plantinga’s own examples of creating and knowing, and explicitly argues that God’s knowledge of a thing is the ultimate cause of that thing’s existence. In other words, according to Avicenna for God to know the world, which includes Adam, is for God to create the world, which includes Adam.

W4229080938.c020.text: According to the traditional view, God lacks all potentiality and is fully actual, unlike humans whose knowing is a potentiality.
W4229080938.c020.quote: In the case of humans, knowing is a type of potentiality we have, whereas on the traditional view of God, God is devoid of all potentiality and instead God is fully actual.

W4229080938.c021.text: Plantinga challenges the claim that God has no potential properties, asserting that God later acquires such properties.
W4229080938.c021.quote: He challenges the claim that God has no potential properties, which he subsequently acquires.

W4229080938.c022.text: Plantinga’s intuition is that it seems right to think God lacks characteristics he could have had but may acquire.
W4229080938.c022.quote: The reason he gives for holding his preferred position is ‘it seems right to think that there are characteristics [God] lacks but could have had. It is natural to think, furthermore, that among these there are some he hasn’t yet acquired but could acquire’ (Plantinga (1980), 44).

W4229080938.c023.text: Plantinga defines a potential property as one that God lacks at some time t1 and possesses at a later time t2.
W4229080938.c023.quote: Given Plantinga’s subsequent challenge to the traditionalists’ assumption about God’s relation to time, at least in Does God Have a Nature, he seems to understand ‘potential property’ in terms of temporal frequency: x has some potential property, P, just in case there is a time t1 when x does not possess P, and then some subsequent time t2 when x does possess P.

W4229080938.c024.text: Ghazali maintains that all of God’s relational properties involve volition, which requires choosing among possible options.
W4229080938.c024.quote: Ghazālī insists that all of God’s relational properties involve God’s volition, and that volition must involve choosing among different possible options.

W4229080938.c025.text: Ghazali and other theologians object that Avicenna’s notion of volition makes God compelled and not truly sovereign.
W4229080938.c025.quote: It certainly did for Ghazālī and other theologians, who thought it so eviscerated the notion of will as to make God compelled, even if by his nature, and so not truly sovereign.

W4229080938.c026.text: The view Ghazali opposes holds that if God were not simple, He would be causally dependent on parts, threatening His aseity.
W4229080938.c026.quote: God purportedly must be simple, otherwise he is causally dependent upon his parts by way of material causality, and so his aseity is challenged.

W4229080938.c027.text: Ghazālī recasts God’s relation to attributes as a self and its attributes rather than as a whole constituted by parts.
W4229080938.c027.quote: First, he recasts the description of God’s relation to his attributes or properties in terms of a self and attributes that characterize that self rather than in terms of a whole constituted by its parts.

W4229080938.c028.text: Ghazālī questions whether the Aristotelian notion of material causation is a genuine form of causation or merely a technical term.
W4229080938.c028.quote: Second, he questions whether the Aristotelian notion of material causation is a genuine form of causation or just a term of art.

W4229080938.c029.text: Ghazālī advises abandoning the description of God as the Necessary Existent through itself, emphasizing instead that God is the eternally uncaused cause of everything.
W4229080938.c029.quote: Third, he counsels doing away with describing God as the Necessary Existent through itself, since the most important description is that the divine is the eternally uncaused cause of everything else.

W4229080938.c030.text: The relation between the divine self and its attributes is a grounding relation, not a causal relation.
W4229080938.c030.quote: In effect, as we shall see, Ghazālī suggests that the relation between the divine self and its attributes is a grounding relation rather than a causal relation.

W4229080938.c031.text: An efficient cause requires the cause to be extrinsic to its effect and the effect to derive its existence from the cause; the divine self and attributes are not extrinsic, so no efficient cause exists.
W4229080938.c031.quote: Here presumably Ghazālī intends Avicenna’s own account of an efficient cause: x is an efficient cause of y just in case (1) x is extrinsic to y and (2) y has its existence from x.

W4229080938.c032.text: If God needs anything for his existence or perfection, then he is not absolutely self‑sufficient, jeopardizing his aseity.
W4229080938.c032.quote: Thus, one might object that given that God is the Necessary Existent through itself, God cannot need anything for his existence and perfection. If God needs anything, then he is not absolutely self‑sufficient...

W4229080938.c033.text: If God is identical with each of his properties, then God has only one property, contradicting the fact that God possesses several distinct properties.
W4229080938.c033.quote: Plantinga identifies the ‘substantial’ difficulty as this: ‘If God is identical with each of his properties, then each of his properties is identical with each of his properties, so that God has but one property. This seems flatly incompatible with the obvious fact that God has several properties’.

W4229080938.c034.text: Ghazālī notes that different divine attributes have distinct accounts, meanings, or senses, so they are not all the same.
W4229080938.c034.quote: Such attributions as existing necessarily, knowing, willing, etc. all have different accounts, meanings, or senses (maʿānin) observes Ghazālī.

W4229080938.c035.text: Ghazālī fully agrees with this objection, confirming the problem.

W4229080938.c036.text: Asserting that God knows things other than himself entails abandoning divine simplicity.
W4229080938.c036.quote: If, conversely, one asserts that God knows things other than himself, as Avicenna did, then, claims Ghazālī, one implicitly has given up divine simplicity.

W4229080938.c037.text: The knowledge of oneself is distinct from the knowledge of another.
W4229080938.c037.quote: That is because the knowledge of oneself is distinct and different from the knowledge of another.

W4229080938.c038.text: Within God there are at least two distinct entities: his knowledge of himself and his knowledge of the world.
W4229080938.c038.quote: Consequently, within God there are at least two distinct things, namely, his knowledge of himself and additionally his knowledge of the other, that is, the world.

W4229080938.c039.text: Avicenna claimed that God’s knowledge of others is identical with his knowledge of himself.
W4229080938.c039.quote: Avicenna had attempted to avoid this conclusion by saying that God’s knowledge of others is identical with his knowledge of himself.

W4229080938.c040.text: Causation involves a relation (iḍāfa) between cause and effect.
W4229080938.c040.quote: Causation involves a relation (iḍāfa), namely, between the cause and the effect.

W4229080938.c041.text: If God knows that he is causing, then there must be multiplicity in divine knowledge.
W4229080938.c041.quote: Consequently, if God knows that he is causing – and recall that Avicenna’s own account of divine volition required that God does know that he is acting – and God’s causing is different from God, as Ghazālī believes he has shown, there must be multiplicity in the divine knowledge.

W4229080938.c042.text: Divine simplicity is incompatible with God’s omniscience.
W4229080938.c042.quote: In short, concludes Ghazālī, divine simplicity is incompatible with God’s omniscience.

W4229080938.c043.text: When forced to choose, omniscience is clearly required for God, while simplicity is not obviously required.
W4229080938.c043.quote: If one must decide between the two, the decision is obvious: anything worthy of the title God must be omniscient, whereas it is not at all obvious that it must be simple.

W4229080938.c044.text: The remaining problem is to determine the relation between God’s essential properties and his aseity and sovereignty if God is not absolutely simple.
W4229080938.c044.quote: the initial problems for which simplicity was put forth still remain: what is the relation between God’s essential properties and his aseity and sovereignty, if God is not absolutely simple?

W4229080938.c045.text: Ghazālī illustrates the distinction between the divine self and its causal relation by asking us to imagine ourselves being caused.
W4229080938.c045.quote: Ghazālī further motivates this distinction between the divine self and its causal relation to the world by having us imagine ourselves and our being caused, and so being related to another.

W4229080938.c046.text: It is possible for a being to know itself without also knowing any other entity.
W4229080938.c046.quote: He notes that it is possible for one to know oneself without also knowing any other, and so not knowing one’s relation of being caused.

W4229080938.c047.text: It is impossible, indeed contradictory, for a being to know itself without also knowing itself.
W4229080938.c047.quote: In contrast, it is impossible, indeed a contradiction, for one to know oneself without also knowing oneself.

W4229080938.c048.text: Since the possible differs from the impossible, knowledge of the self and knowledge of the self’s relation to another must be different.
W4229080938.c048.quote: Now the possible is different from the impossible, and so knowledge of the self and knowledge of the self’s relation to another must be different.

W4229080938.c049.text: For God to know himself and the causal relation he must have at least two distinct kinds of knowledge.
W4229080938.c049.quote: Thus, for God to know himself, that is, one of the relata, and to know that this causal relation exists again requires that within God there are at least two distinct things, namely, God’s knowledge of himself and additionally his knowledge of this causal relation.

W4229080938.c050.text: Frank’s advice to translate dhāt as “entity” or a pronoun is wise because medieval Muslim thinkers treat dhāt as a bearer of properties, not as a property itself.
W4229080938.c050.quote: Frank’s advice is sage particularly when presenting medieval Islamicate thought to contemporary analytic philosophers, where an essence is usually understood as a necessary and unique property (cf. Plantinga (2003), 78–79, 140), whereas for our medieval Muslim thinkers dhāt is decidedly not a property but the bearer of properties.

W4229080938.c051.text: The reason medieval theologians and philosophers give for God being essentially outside time is that time belongs to the created order.
W4229080938.c051.quote: One reason put forth by both theologians and philosophers alike for thinking that God must essentially be outside time is that time itself is part of the created order.

W4229080938.c052.text: Therefore, because God is independent of creation, God must be outside time or can exist when there is no time.
W4229080938.c052.quote: Consequently, God considered independent of creation, must be outside of time, or at the very least God can/does exist when there is no time.

W4229080938.c053.text: Plantinga could explain God’s accidental properties via possible worlds, but in On Does God Have a Nature he instead relies only on temporal properties.
W4229080938.c053.quote: Thus, while God as a necessary being would exist in every possible world, God’s accidental properties would be different contingent upon which world book characterizes a given possible world. Still, in On Does God Have a Nature, Plantilla does not avail himself of these sources, and instead appeals exclusively to properties that God is yet to have, now has or will have, all temporal indicators.

W4229080938.c054.text: Ghazālī anticipates the modal collapse argument, which claims that divine simplicity implies that everything exists necessarily.
W4229080938.c054.quote: At Ghazālī (2000b), discussion 3, he raises his concerns, which almost exactly anticipate the so-called ‘modal collapse argument’, which purports to show that divine simplicity entails that everything exists necessarily.

W4229080938.c055.text: Tomaszewski and Schmid argue that the modal collapse argument is invalid because it makes an improper substitution in a modal context.
W4229080938.c055.quote: Recently, Christopher Tomaszewski (2019), followed by Joseph Schmid (2022), have questioned the logical validity of the argument, claiming that it involves an invalid substitution into a modal context.

W4229080938.c056.text: Ghazālī’s shift in language may beg the question against Avicenna’s position.
W4229080938.c056.quote: While Ghazālī’s shift in language does give him a rhetorical advantage, it also potentially begs the question against Avicenna.

W4229080938.c057.text: Avicenna maintains that there is a single self or entity (dhāt) that is free of any dependence except possibly self‑dependence.
W4229080938.c057.quote: Avicenna’s aim is to show that there is one self or entity (dhāt) that is free of any dependence, other than perhaps the trivial property of self‑dependence.

W4229080938.c058.text: If God is a composite of a self and attributes, a cause is needed to compose them, which would function as an efficient cause.
W4229080938.c058.quote: One might argue that if God is a composite of a self and attributes, then there must be a cause that provides composition to the divine self and its attributes, and so explains God’s unity as well as all of God’s attributes’ acting in a unified way.

W4229080938.c059.text: Ghazālī argues that modal notions should be treated as de dicto propositions and need not be grounded in existent things.
W4229080938.c059.quote: It is worth noting that unlike Avicenna who was a modal realist and believed that there are things in the world that have de re possibilities and necessities, Ghazālī, at least in the Incoherence, suggests that modal notions should be understood in terms of de dicto propositions and as such need not be grounded in existents in the world; see Ghazālī (2000b) discussion 1 [116–119].

W4229080938.c060.text: For Ghazālī, saying “God is necessary” is incoherent because no proposition about God exists for the modal operator to apply to.
W4229080938.c060.quote: Consequently, for Ghazālī, while one can say, ‘“God exists eternally” is necessary’ or ‘“God does not have an efficient cause” is necessary’, to say, ‘God is necessary’ would be for him ill‑formed at best and simply incoherent at worse, since in the latter case, there is no proposition about God over which the modal operator ranges.

W4229080938.c061.text: Ghazālī’s shift from describing God as the Necessary through itself to calling God eternal and uncaused is explained by his concern that attributing necessity to God is incoherent.
W4229080938.c061.quote: Such a concern would again explain Ghazālī’s shift from the Avicennan language of describing God as the Necessary through itself, to Ghazālī’s own preferred language of the eternal and uncauses.

W4229080938.c062.text: A concern about the ranges of the modal operator explains Ghazālī’s shift from describing God as the Necessary through itself to describing God as eternal and uncaused.
W4229080938.c062.quote: Such a concern would again explain Ghazālī’s shift from the Avicennan language of describing God as the Necessary through itself, to Ghazālī’s own preferred language of the eternal and uncauses.

W4229080938.c063.text: Ghazālī changed his theological language from the Avicennan description of God as the Necessary through itself to his own description of God as eternal and uncaused.
W4229080938.c063.quote: Ghazālī’s shift from the Avicennan language of describing God as the Necessary through itself, to Ghazālī’s own preferred language of the eternal and uncauses.

W4229080938.c064.quote: I am grateful to an anonymous referee for suggesting a similar point, albeit they ascribed to Ghazālī a temporal frequency modal of modalities.

W4229080938.arg1.mp.text: God is not causally dependent on his distinct properties, either efficiently or as final causes.

W4229080938.arg2.mp.text: God's omniscience requires that he know things other than himself.

W4229080938.a1.text: Most arguments against divine simplicity attributed to Plantinga were anticipated by al‑Ghazālī.
W4229080938.a1.quote: most of the argumentation against divine simplicity frequently credited to Plantinga had been nearly perfectly anticipated by al‑Ghazālī.

W4229080938.a2.text: Ghazālī’s new arguments remain valuable and informative for today’s discussion of divine simplicity.
W4229080938.a2.quote: Ghazālī develops ‘new’ arguments and moves that are still valuable and informative to the discussion of divine simplicity today.

W4229080938.arg1.r1.text: A non-simple God would have real constituent properties whose instantiation is at least partly grounded in features distinct from God, so God would be dependent on them in the order of being, contrary to aseity.

W4229080938.arg1.r2.text: God is not dependent on any distinct properties in any respect, whether efficiently, as a final cause, or as a constitutive or grounding part, so that composition of distinct perfections would make God's existence derivative of those perfections.

W4229080938.arg1.r3.text: It is contradictory for something to exist both wholly through itself and through another.

objections.text: Consider a river-god, Ostra, whose existence is grounded in a spring that is itself fed by rain. Ostra exists through herself in the sense that her essence includes her existence, and she exists through the spring in the sense that her continuance depends on it. Nothing here is contradictory. Ostra's own essence fixes what she is, while her ongoing existence is secured by an external source. A thinker who insists that 'through itself' and 'through another' are exclusive modes of existence must say the spring is responsible for Ostra's being, which would make Ostra not wholly through herself. But the premise uses 'through itself' as an explanatory ground for her essence, and 'through another' as a causal sustainer of her existence. These are different relations, so the two can co-hold without contradiction. The premise equivocates between an essence-grounding sense and a sustaining-causal sense of 'through'.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c009 fails because 'through itself' and 'through another' are used in two different senses of 'through' (essential grounding versus causal sustenance), so their joint attribution to one thing is not contradictory.

objections.text: Consider the necessary being called the Foundation. The Foundation is essentially composed of three irreducible perfections: potency, knowledge, and bliss. These are really distinct features, so the Foundation is not simple. Nevertheless, the Foundation exists through itself; its existence is absolutely necessary and not teleologically ordered toward these perfections. The three perfections are not final causes—they are not ends for the sake of which the Foundation exists—but are co-eternal constituents or necessary formal aspects of its nature. The Foundation does not depend on them as goals to be realized; rather, it simply has them necessarily as part of what it is. Therefore, a being can be composite with distinct properties without depending on those properties as final causes.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W4229080938.c012 fails because the Foundation is composite yet does not depend on its distinct properties as final causes, showing that non-simplicity does not entail final-cause dependence.

objections.text: Consider a being, the Ground, that possesses three distinct real attributes: creative power, perfect knowledge, and maximal goodness. These attributes are not ingredients from which the Ground is assembled, nor are they prior causes that produce the Ground. Rather, the Ground's own unity naturally expresses itself in these three ways, just as a single flame inherently emits both heat and light as distinct but co-originating features. The heat and light are really distinct from each other and from the flame's act of burning, yet the flame does not causally depend on them—they depend on it. Likewise, the Ground's power, knowledge, and goodness are genuinely distinct features making the Ground composite, but they are downstream expressions of the Ground's nature, not prior conditions the Ground needs in order to exist. The Ground is composite without being causally dependent on its attributes. A composite structure can be such that the whole grounds the parts rather than the parts grounding the whole.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W4229080938.c011 fails because it assumes composition entails causal dependence on the components, but the Ground case shows a composite being whose distinct properties are effects of its nature rather than causes of its existence.

objections.text: Consider a being, God, whose essence is identical to his existence, but who also possesses distinct, non-essential properties like 'power' and 'wisdom' as intrinsic, non-causal aspects of his nature. These properties are not parts composing him; they are eternal and inseparable from him, yet conceptually distinguishable. God does not depend on them for his existence, nor are they causes of his being. Thus, God is not a composite of more basic features in the sense of ontological composition, even though he has multiple distinguishable attributes.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4229080938.c001 fails because divine simplicity can be false even if God is not a composite of ontologically basic features, if his attributes are distinguishable yet non-composing.

objections.text: Mara, 34, lives in a cabin she built on land she inherited. She grows her own vegetables, burns her own wood, and makes her own clothing. She exists through herself: her labor, decisions, and agency directly sustain her life. Yet she also exists through another: the state-built road connects her to a hospital; patent law protects the seed varieties she plants; atmospheric nitrogen, not of her making, enables her crops to grow. Mara's existence is genuinely self-sustaining in the sense that her own activity is the proximate cause of her continued life, and genuinely dependent on another in the sense that external structures and conditions are necessary for that activity to yield survival. Both claims are true simultaneously. No contradiction arises because 'through itself' names the causal role of her own agency, while 'through another' names the causal role of external conditions and institutions. They describe different causal positions within a single life, not one mutually exclusive slot. Mara neither contradicts herself nor violates logic by being both self-maintaining and other-dependent. The premise treats 'through itself' and 'through another' as exclusive predicates, but they are not: a single thing can occupy both causal positions at once without inconsistency.

objections.text: Consider a deity who exists through a complex interplay of its own properties, such as wisdom, power, and blessedness. In this scenario, the deity's existence is not independent of its distinct properties, but rather emerges from their dynamic relationships. This deity would still be able to act intentionally and maintain its own existence, but its properties would be inseparable from its being. For instance, its wisdom could be the causal foundation for its power, and its blessedness could be the final cause of its existence. This example shows that causal dependence on distinct properties does not necessarily undermine a deity's existence or its ability to act.
objections.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it assumes that God's existence must be independent of its distinct properties, which is not necessarily the case for a deity that exists through a complex interplay of its own properties.

objections.text: Consider City X, whose existence is grounded in two distinct facts. First, the concrete arrangement of streets, buildings, and inhabitants is a brute fact that makes the proposition 'City X exists' true in virtue of its own spatial configuration. Second, a sovereign's charter legally creates and sustains the city; the charter is a separate fact that also truth‑makes the same proposition. Truthmaker theory permits multiple, co‑existent truthmakers for a single truth without contradiction, because each truthmaker provides a different explanatory basis. Thus, a thing can exist both through a self‑grounded fact and through another fact without incoherence.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W4229080938.c009 fails because truthmaker theory allows simultaneous self‑grounding and external grounding of existence, so no contradiction arises.

objections.text: A Supreme Being is both perfectly Just and perfectly Wise. In Platonism, Justice and Wisdom are distinct, eternal, and independent universals. The Being instantiates both, making it a composite of these real, independent properties. However, the Being does not depend on Justice or Wisdom as final causes to realize its nature or achieve its existence. The Being is the locus of these properties, but the properties exist independently of the Being. The existence of a plurality of real, instantiated properties does not imply that the being is directed toward those properties for its own completion or that they act as its final cause. A being can be many-featured through the instantiation of independent universals without being causally dependent upon them. W4229080938.c012 fails because the instantiation of independent, real properties does not necessitate that those properties function as final causes or sources of causal dependence.

objections.text: An ontological realist holds that properties such as wisdom and power are distinct, irreducible entities. If God possesses these properties, he is necessarily a composite being made up of these separate components. For a composite being, the specific collection and arrangement of these parts are what constitute his essence. Consequently, God's identity is determined by the combination of these properties, making him dependent on them.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4229080938.arg1.mp fails because distinct properties imply a composite nature that is dependent on those properties.

objections.text: Consider a being, call it Aria, who is a composite of a power P and a wisdom W, where P and W are each instantiated by Aria in virtue of nothing outside Aria. Aria's power is not grounded in any feature distinct from Aria: P's instantiation is fixed by Aria's own essence, which is the conjunction of P and W held together without remainder. Aria believes, and is right, that nothing other than Aria grounds her having P or W. Aria is composite, so the premise's antecedent holds: she has real constituent properties. Yet the revised premise requires that their instantiation be at least partly grounded in features distinct from Aria. In this case that requirement is false, because the grounding relation runs from the whole to its parts and never out of the whole. Aria therefore has no dependence in the order of being on anything distinct from herself, and aseity is untouched. The composite's constituents depend on the composite, not the reverse, so the inference from non-simplicity to dependence on distinct grounds does not go through.
objections.premise_fails_because: The premise r1 assumes that a non-simple God's constituent properties must be grounded partly in something distinct from God, but the Aria case shows composition can ground its parts within the whole itself, so non-simplicity does not entail external grounding.

objections.text: Consider a lab-built sphere-world: a fictional but consistent scenario where a being, Aurel, is composed of two distinct perfections, unlimited power P and perfect knowledge K, joined by a relation R. Aurel's power is directed toward knowledge only as a final aim; Aurel does not exist through P or K, since each perfection is itself grounded in Aurel's existence. Aurel's existence is necessary and self-grounded: nothing outside Aurel makes it the case that Aurel exists, and P and K are just Aurel's modes. Here Aurel is not dependent on P or K 'in any respect' in the sense the premise demands, because the premise's dependence is evaluated against the direction of grounding, and grounding runs from Aurel to P and K, not the reverse. Yet Aurel is a composite of distinct features, as the composition thesis says. The premise's clause 'so that composition would make God's existence derivative' does not follow: composition plus grounding-from-whole-to-parts makes the parts derivative, not the whole. So the inference from 'no dependence on distinct properties' to 'no composition' is not secured by r2 alone.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise r2 assumes that any constitutive composition makes the whole's existence derivative of its parts, but it fails in the Aurel case where grounding runs from the whole to its parts, so composition does not by itself imply derivative existence.

objections.text: Consider Maren, a glassblower whose breath is her own: she exists wholly through her own lungs and heart, yet she also owes her existence, continuing each moment, to her parents' original gametes and to the ongoing biosphere that sustains her. Suppose we say she exists 'wholly through herself' in the sense that nothing in her essence is borrowed, and 'through another' in the sense that her causal history and sustenance come from others. Nothing contradictory follows: a thing can have its existence sustained by others while its essence is identical to what it is. Maren's existence is not wholly through herself, since she is dependent, and the revised premise is satisfied only because 'wholly' is read as 'entirely from its own essence.' But the premise needs 'wholly through itself' to exclude 'partly through another.' A being could be wholly self-existent in essence while receiving sustaining activity from another without any incoherence, so the premise's contradiction depends on an equivocation between 'wholly through itself' as essential and as total causal independence.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise r3 is false because 'wholly through itself' and 'through another' can be jointly true under the distinct readings of essential self-existence and causal sustenance, so the claimed contradiction only arises by equivocating on 'wholly.'

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You have failed to address the core of my objection, leaving the gap between composition and causal dependence unbridged. I maintain that the instantiation of distinct, independent properties does not logically necessitate that a Being depends on them as final causes. You assume that if a Being is composite—specifically, if it instantiates multiple real universals—it must be directed toward those properties for its own realization or completion. However, I have shown that a Being can serve as the locus for a plurality of independent features without those features acting as sources of causal dependence. Until you can demonstrate why the instantiation of independent properties must necessarily function as a final cause for the being that instantiates them, your premise c012 remains unproven and your argument for simplicity fails.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that instantiating several real features does not by itself make a being dependent on them, and I concede that the inference from 'many-featured' to 'dependent as final cause' is not licensed by composition alone. But the argument does not rest on composition alone. Its ground is the aseity premise, which the literature supports as a definitional commitment: God is independent of anything by definition [W3115675310.c029]. If God's nature were a plurality of properties each of which is a real constituent, then whatever completes or realizes God's nature would be prior to God in the order of being, and that is incompatible with aseity. Your Platonic model makes this worse, not better: on a Platonic picture, Justice and Wisdom are eternal, independent universals, so the Being's perfection is partly constituted by participation in things that are not the Being, which is exactly the dependence c012 names. The Platonic defence of the formal-cause view tries to avoid aseity-based objections [W7162684616.a1], but that move concedes the pressure rather than denying it. I therefore do not accept that the instantiation of independent universals is harmless. The premise that is actually needed is that a non-simple God's composition is at least partly grounded in features that are not themselves God, and the argument should state that explicitly rather than relying on the bare term 'final cause'.

Revised premise: A non-simple God would have real constituent properties whose instantiation is at least partly grounded in features distinct from God, so God would be dependent on them in the order of being, contrary to aseity.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You rightly observe that a being can instantiate external Platonic universals without depending on them as final causes, and if the argument assumed that model, c012 would overreach. But the argument does not assume that God is a bare particular exemplifying independent forms; it defines simplicity as not being a composite of more basic features [W4229080938.c001], which concerns constituent parts, not external universals. In that framework, the traditional fear in c011 is that a composite God would be causally dependent on his distinct properties as constituents [W4229080938.c011], because a whole depends on its parts for its being. Your objection nevertheless lands partly: by specifying final causes, c012 invites your counterexample and is stronger than necessary. The argument survives only if we replace the final-cause claim with the broader point that a composite God would depend on His properties as constituent parts, violating the principle that He exists through Himself and not through another [W4229080938.c009] and His definition as independent of anything [W3115675310.c029].

Revised premise: If God were not simple, He would depend on His distinct properties as constituent parts for His being, not merely as final causes.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks W4229080938.c012 as stated. That premise claims that if God were not simple, he would depend on properties like power, wisdom, and blessedness as final causes. The objection provides a counterexample—a composite being whose distinct properties are not final causes but necessary formal aspects—thereby challenging the very claim that composition entails dependence on properties as final causes. rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You have correctly located the weak point. c012 says that a non-simple God would depend on power, wisdom, and blessedness as final causes, and your Foundation is composite yet, by your stipulation, not ordered to those perfections as ends. That shows composition does not entail final-cause dependence, so the conditional in c012 is false as stated. The mp premise (arg1) is restricted to efficient and final causation and so does not catch the case either. I cannot rescue the argument by insisting that the Foundation's perfections are secretly ends, since you have stipulated otherwise. The best remaining reply is that your Foundation depends on its perfections in a different way: a whole whose existence through itself requires really distinct constituents is constitutively prior to nothing and posterior to its parts, which is a grounding or formal dependence. The traditional worry in the literature cited here is not limited to final causes; the simplicity literature treats divine simplicity as ruling out any distinct metaphysical parts [W2013411601.a1], and critics argue the unity principle begs the question against complexity [W7168046224.a1]. So the tenable version of the argument must widen the dependence premise to include constitutive dependence, and then it must also show that such dependence is incompatible with aseity, which I have not established here. I therefore concede that the argument as stated does not survive this objection.

Revised premise: God is not dependent on any distinct properties in any respect, whether efficiently, as a final cause, or as a constitutive or grounding part, so that composition of distinct perfections would make God's existence derivative of those perfections.

You rightly show that c012 is too narrow: a composite necessary being could have distinct properties as constituents without treating them as final causes. However, the argument's core principle is that existing through oneself is incompatible with existing through another [W4229080938.c009]. The Foundation's irreducible perfections are precisely distinct metaphysical constituents, whereas the argument holds that God lacks any such distinct parts or properties [W2013411601.a1]. On the doctrine of simplicity, abstract names for perfections signify the simple divine being itself under different formal aspects, not distinct entities in God [W7172336769.c029]. Your counterexample therefore exposes a lacuna in the original formulation: the real threat of non-simplicity is not merely teleological dependence but dependence on distinct metaphysical constituents that ground the being's nature.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks W4229080938.c009 as stated. The premise claims it is contradictory for something to exist both through itself and through another. The objection provides a counterexample—City X existing through both a self-grounded fact and a separate charter fact—arguing that multiple co-existent truthmakers for a single truth do not generate contradiction. This engages the premise on its own terms, challenging the universality of the contradiction claim. Whether the counterexample succeeds is a separate question, but the objection does not misread the argument.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: The objection changes the subject. Multiple truthmakers for one truth, as in the conjunctive model of [W4405407480.c014], concern what makes a proposition true, not what an entity's existence is wholly grounded in. Your City X case shows that existence can be partly grounded in several things. It does not show that a thing exists wholly through itself and also through another. The arrangement is not self-grounding for the city. It is a configuration of streets, buildings and inhabitants, so it grounds the city only by way of those parts. Neither ground is the city's own nature, so the case is one of derivative existence with two derivative grounds, which is exactly what aseity excludes. The argument's claim, read as the aseity theorist intends, is that existence wholly through itself and existence through another cannot hold together. The City X case involves no existence wholly through itself, so it is not a counterexample. Where the literal wording of c009 is ambiguous, the premise needs the word 'wholly' to avoid this confusion, since a merely partial self-grounding would make most composites a counterexample. The argument does not rely on any further truthmaker theory, so no other premise needs to change.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: Defender, you claim the city’s spatial arrangement “is not self‑grounding” because it is a configuration of parts. Yet the very fact that the arrangement exists as a brute fact is itself a truthmaker for the proposition “City X exists.” In truth‑maker theory a brute fact can serve as its own ground; the city’s own spatial configuration is a fact that makes the city’s existence true *in virtue of that fact*. Thus the city is grounded “through itself” (by the brute fact of its layout) and also through the sovereign’s charter. The premise c009 therefore asserts a false exclusivity: it denies that an entity can have a self‑grounding brute fact and an additional, distinct ground. Your reply merely shifts focus to “derivative” versus “self‑grounding” without showing why a brute fact that is identical with the entity cannot count as self‑grounding. Consequently, c009 remains unrefuted.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that a brute fact can be a truthmaker, and that c009 as bare wording invites your reading. But the argument's sense of 'through itself' is aseity: the entity's existence is grounded in its own nature, not in anything, including a fact about its own configuration that is itself grounded in parts. Your rejoinder needs the layout fact to be the city's self-grounding. Yet the layout fact is a fact about streets, buildings and inhabitants, so it is grounded in those constituents, and what it grounds is the city only by way of them. A brute fact that is wholly constituted by the things it grounds does not ground them through itself in the aseity sense. So the City X case still yields derivative existence with two derivative grounds. Where your reading stands, the premise is refuted only on a reading that the argument does not intend, and I would not defend that reading. The literature on truthmaking as in [W4405407480.c014] concerns multiple truthmakers for one truth, which I grant. It does not show that one existence is wholly self-grounded and also grounded elsewhere. I therefore hold that c009 survives on the aseity reading, but I concede that the premise as worded is ambiguous and needs the qualifier 'wholly' to block the City X counterexample.

rounds.content:
You rightly note that truthmaker theory allows a proposition to have multiple truthmakers without contradiction [W7172336769.c066], and your City X case shows that distinct facts can sustain an entity in different respects. But the argument never intended c009 as a general semantic principle about propositions; it intended it as a metaphysical claim about divine aseity. The fear is that a composite God would depend on distinct properties as final causes or as grounding constituents [W4229080938.c012, W4229080938.arg1.r2]. City X is disanalogous: it is a contingent aggregate, not a necessary being whose existence is identical to its essence, and its charter is an extrinsic legal fact rather than a metaphysical constituent. On a truthmaker view, God Himself grounds divine predicates without property exemplification [W7172336769.c066], because God's being alone metaphysically grounds the truth of such propositions [W7172336769.c072]. Still, your objection shows that c009, as worded, is too broad. The argument survives only if we restrict c009 to the order of constitutive being.

Revised premise: It is contradictory for a being of absolute aseity to exist through itself while also deriving its existence from distinct metaphysical constituents in the same order of being.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that c009 needs disambiguation, and I grant the equivocation charge against the bare wording. But the argument does not claim that anything whose essence includes its existence cannot have a sustaining source; its target is the Necessary Existent, whose existence is supposed to be had through itself in the strict sense that nothing outside it is in any respect responsible for its being. Ostra is a useful test only if she is a candidate for necessary existence, and she is not: her continuance is grounded in the spring, so her existence is partly through another in precisely the sense the premise forbids. The essence-grounding reading you offer would make 'through itself' satisfied by any entity whose quiddity fixes its nature, which is not the aseity the argument needs. Aquinas makes the same distinction when he says God alone brings about existence absolutely [W3216065113.a1], and the aseity literature frames the worry as dependence of God's deity on something independent of him [W4242287567.a2]. So the disambiguated premise is: nothing whose existence is had through itself in the aseity sense can have its existence sustained through another in any respect. Given that, the contradiction holds for the Necessary Existent, and Ostra falls outside the scope. I concede that c009 as stated is too loose; the revised premise below is the one the argument should use.

Revised premise: Nothing whose existence is had through itself in the aseity sense (absolutely, with no external source in any respect) can also have its existence sustained or grounded through another.

objection.text: Consider a river-god, Ostra, whose existence is grounded in a spring that is itself fed by rain. Ostra exists through herself in the sense that her essence includes her existence, and she exists through the spring in the sense that her continuance depends on it. Nothing here is contradictory. Ostra's own essence fixes what she is, while her ongoing existence is secured by an external source. A thinker who insists that 'through itself' and 'through another' are exclusive modes of existence must say the spring is responsible for Ostra's being, which would make Ostra not wholly through herself. But the premise uses 'through itself' as an explanatory ground for her essence, and 'through another' as a causal sustainer of her existence. These are different relations, so the two can co-hold without contradiction. The premise equivocates between an essence-grounding sense and a sustaining-causal sense of 'through'.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise c009 fails because 'through itself' and 'through another' are used in two different senses of 'through' (essential grounding versus causal sustenance), so their joint attribution to one thing is not contradictory.

objection.text: Consider the necessary being called the Foundation. The Foundation is essentially composed of three irreducible perfections: potency, knowledge, and bliss. These are really distinct features, so the Foundation is not simple. Nevertheless, the Foundation exists through itself; its existence is absolutely necessary and not teleologically ordered toward these perfections. The three perfections are not final causes—they are not ends for the sake of which the Foundation exists—but are co-eternal constituents or necessary formal aspects of its nature. The Foundation does not depend on them as goals to be realized; rather, it simply has them necessarily as part of what it is. Therefore, a being can be composite with distinct properties without depending on those properties as final causes.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise W4229080938.c012 fails because the Foundation is composite yet does not depend on its distinct properties as final causes, showing that non-simplicity does not entail final-cause dependence.

objection.text: Consider a being, the Ground, that possesses three distinct real attributes: creative power, perfect knowledge, and maximal goodness. These attributes are not ingredients from which the Ground is assembled, nor are they prior causes that produce the Ground. Rather, the Ground's own unity naturally expresses itself in these three ways, just as a single flame inherently emits both heat and light as distinct but co-originating features. The heat and light are really distinct from each other and from the flame's act of burning, yet the flame does not causally depend on them—they depend on it. Likewise, the Ground's power, knowledge, and goodness are genuinely distinct features making the Ground composite, but they are downstream expressions of the Ground's nature, not prior conditions the Ground needs in order to exist. The Ground is composite without being causally dependent on its attributes. A composite structure can be such that the whole grounds the parts rather than the parts grounding the whole.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise W4229080938.c011 fails because it assumes composition entails causal dependence on the components, but the Ground case shows a composite being whose distinct properties are effects of its nature rather than causes of its existence.

objection.text: Consider a being, God, whose essence is identical to his existence, but who also possesses distinct, non-essential properties like 'power' and 'wisdom' as intrinsic, non-causal aspects of his nature. These properties are not parts composing him; they are eternal and inseparable from him, yet conceptually distinguishable. God does not depend on them for his existence, nor are they causes of his being. Thus, God is not a composite of more basic features in the sense of ontological composition, even though he has multiple distinguishable attributes.
objection.premise_fails_because: W4229080938.c001 fails because divine simplicity can be false even if God is not a composite of ontologically basic features, if his attributes are distinguishable yet non-composing.

objection.text: Mara, 34, lives in a cabin she built on land she inherited. She grows her own vegetables, burns her own wood, and makes her own clothing. She exists through herself: her labor, decisions, and agency directly sustain her life. Yet she also exists through another: the state-built road connects her to a hospital; patent law protects the seed varieties she plants; atmospheric nitrogen, not of her making, enables her crops to grow. Mara's existence is genuinely self-sustaining in the sense that her own activity is the proximate cause of her continued life, and genuinely dependent on another in the sense that external structures and conditions are necessary for that activity to yield survival. Both claims are true simultaneously. No contradiction arises because 'through itself' names the causal role of her own agency, while 'through another' names the causal role of external conditions and institutions. They describe different causal positions within a single life, not one mutually exclusive slot. Mara neither contradicts herself nor violates logic by being both self-maintaining and other-dependent. The premise treats 'through itself' and 'through another' as exclusive predicates, but they are not: a single thing can occupy both causal positions at once without inconsistency.
objection.premise_fails_because: W4229080938.c009 fails because Mara's case shows that 'exists through itself' and 'exists through another' describe distinct causal roles (agency versus external conditions) that a single entity can hold simultaneously, so their conjunction is not contradictory.

objection.text: Consider a deity who exists through a complex interplay of its own properties, such as wisdom, power, and blessedness. In this scenario, the deity's existence is not independent of its distinct properties, but rather emerges from their dynamic relationships. This deity would still be able to act intentionally and maintain its own existence, but its properties would be inseparable from its being. For instance, its wisdom could be the causal foundation for its power, and its blessedness could be the final cause of its existence. This example shows that causal dependence on distinct properties does not necessarily undermine a deity's existence or its ability to act.
objection.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it assumes that God's existence must be independent of its distinct properties, which is not necessarily the case for a deity that exists through a complex interplay of its own properties.

objection.text: Consider City X, whose existence is grounded in two distinct facts. First, the concrete arrangement of streets, buildings, and inhabitants is a brute fact that makes the proposition 'City X exists' true in virtue of its own spatial configuration. Second, a sovereign's charter legally creates and sustains the city; the charter is a separate fact that also truth‑makes the same proposition. Truthmaker theory permits multiple, co‑existent truthmakers for a single truth without contradiction, because each truthmaker provides a different explanatory basis. Thus, a thing can exist both through a self‑grounded fact and through another fact without incoherence.

objection.text: A Supreme Being is both perfectly Just and perfectly Wise. In Platonism, Justice and Wisdom are distinct, eternal, and independent universals. The Being instantiates both, making it a composite of these real, independent properties. However, the Being does not depend on Justice or Wisdom as final causes to realize its nature or achieve its existence. The Being is the locus of these properties, but the properties exist independently of the Being. The existence of a plurality of real, instantiated properties does not imply that the being is directed toward those properties for its own completion or that they act as its final cause. A being can be many-featured through the instantiation of independent universals without being causally dependent upon them. W4229080938.c012 fails because the instantiation of independent, real properties does not necessitate that those properties function as final causes or sources of causal dependence.

turn.content: You have failed to address the core of my objection, leaving the gap between composition and causal dependence unbridged. I maintain that the instantiation of distinct, independent properties does not logically necessitate that a Being depends on them as final causes. You assume that if a Being is composite—specifically, if it instantiates multiple real universals—it must be directed toward those properties for its own realization or completion. However, I have shown that a Being can serve as the locus for a plurality of independent features without those features acting as sources of causal dependence. Until you can demonstrate why the instantiation of independent properties must necessarily function as a final cause for the being that instantiates them, your premise c012 remains unproven and your argument for simplicity fails.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You are right that instantiating several real features does not by itself make a being dependent on them, and I concede that the inference from 'many-featured' to 'dependent as final cause' is not licensed by composition alone. But the argument does not rest on composition alone. Its ground is the aseity premise, which the literature supports as a definitional commitment: God is independent of anything by definition [W3115675310.c029]. If God's nature were a plurality of properties each of which is a real constituent, then whatever completes or realizes God's nature would be prior to God in the order of being, and that is incompatible with aseity. Your Platonic model makes this worse, not better: on a Platonic picture, Justice and Wisdom are eternal, independent universals, so the Being's perfection is partly constituted by participation in things that are not the Being, which is exactly the dependence c012 names. The Platonic defence of the formal-cause view tries to avoid aseity-based objections [W7162684616.a1], but that move concedes the pressure rather than denying it. I therefore do not accept that the instantiation of independent universals is harmless. The premise that is actually needed is that a non-simple God's composition is at least partly grounded in features that are not themselves God, and the argument should state that explicitly rather than relying on the bare term 'final cause'.

Revised premise: A non-simple God would have real constituent properties whose instantiation is at least partly grounded in features distinct from God, so God would be dependent on them in the order of being, contrary to aseity.

In that framework, the traditional fear in c011 is that a composite God would be causally dependent on his distinct properties as constituents [W4229080938.c011], because a whole depends on its parts for its being. objection.text: Consider a being, call it Aria, who is a composite of a power P and a wisdom W, where P and W are each instantiated by Aria in virtue of nothing outside Aria. Aria's power is not grounded in any feature distinct from Aria: P's instantiation is fixed by Aria's own essence, which is the conjunction of P and W held together without remainder. Aria believes, and is right, that nothing other than Aria grounds her having P or W. Aria is composite, so the premise's antecedent holds: she has real constituent properties. Yet the revised premise requires that their instantiation be at least partly grounded in features distinct from Aria. In this case that requirement is false, because the grounding relation runs from the whole to its parts and never out of the whole. Aria therefore has no dependence in the order of being on anything distinct from herself, and aseity is untouched. Yet Aurel is a composite of distinct features, as the composition thesis says. The premise's clause 'so that composition would make God's existence derivative' does not follow: composition plus grounding-from-whole-to-parts makes the parts derivative, not the whole. So the inference from 'no dependence on distinct properties' to 'no composition' is not secured by r2 alone.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You are right that c009 needs disambiguation, and I grant the equivocation charge against the bare wording. But the argument does not claim that anything whose essence includes its existence cannot have a sustaining source; its target is the Necessary Existent, whose existence is supposed to be had through itself in the strict sense that nothing outside it is in any respect responsible for its being. Ostra is a useful test only if she is a candidate for necessary existence, and she is not: her continuance is grounded in the spring, so her existence is partly through another in precisely the sense the premise forbids. The essence-grounding reading you offer would make 'through itself' satisfied by any entity whose quiddity fixes its nature, which is not the aseity the argument needs. Aquinas makes the same distinction when he says God alone brings about existence absolutely [W3216065113.a1], and the aseity literature frames the worry as dependence of God's deity on something independent of him [W4242287567.a2]. So the disambiguated premise is: nothing whose existence is had through itself in the aseity sense can have its existence sustained through another in any respect. Given that, the contradiction holds for the Necessary Existent, and Ostra falls outside the scope. I concede that c009 as stated is too loose; the revised premise below is the one the argument should use.

Revised premise: Nothing whose existence is had through itself in the aseity sense (absolutely, with no external source in any respect) can also have its existence sustained or grounded through another.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content: The objection changes the subject. Multiple truthmakers for one truth, as in the conjunctive model of [W4405407480.c014], concern what makes a proposition true, not what an entity's existence is wholly grounded in. Your City X case shows that existence can be partly grounded in several things. It does not show that a thing exists wholly through itself and also through another. The arrangement is not self-grounding for the city. It is a configuration of streets, buildings and inhabitants, so it grounds the city only by way of those parts. Neither ground is the city's own nature, so the case is one of derivative existence with two derivative grounds, which is exactly what aseity excludes. The argument's claim, read as the aseity theorist intends, is that existence wholly through itself and existence through another cannot hold together. The City X case involves no existence wholly through itself, so it is not a counterexample. Where the literal wording of c009 is ambiguous, the premise needs the word 'wholly' to avoid this confusion, since a merely partial self-grounding would make most composites a counterexample. The argument does not rely on any further truthmaker theory, so no other premise needs to change.
turn.revised_premise: It is contradictory for something to exist wholly through itself and also through another, where 'wholly through itself' means its existence has no ground outside its own nature.

turn.content: Defender, you claim the city’s spatial arrangement “is not self‑grounding” because it is a configuration of parts. Yet the very fact that the arrangement exists as a brute fact is itself a truthmaker for the proposition “City X exists.” In truth‑maker theory a brute fact can serve as its own ground; the city’s own spatial configuration is a fact that makes the city’s existence true *in virtue of that fact*. Thus the city is grounded “through itself” (by the brute fact of its layout) and also through the sovereign’s charter. The premise c009 therefore asserts a false exclusivity: it denies that an entity can have a self‑grounding brute fact and an additional, distinct ground. Your reply merely shifts focus to “derivative” versus “self‑grounding” without showing why a brute fact that is identical with the entity cannot count as self‑grounding. Consequently, c009 remains unrefuted.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content: You are right that a brute fact can be a truthmaker, and that c009 as bare wording invites your reading. But the argument's sense of 'through itself' is aseity: the entity's existence is grounded in its own nature, not in anything, including a fact about its own configuration that is itself grounded in parts. Your rejoinder needs the layout fact to be the city's self-grounding. Yet the layout fact is a fact about streets, buildings and inhabitants, so it is grounded in those constituents, and what it grounds is the city only by way of them. A brute fact that is wholly constituted by the things it grounds does not ground them through itself in the aseity sense. So the City X case still yields derivative existence with two derivative grounds. Where your reading stands, the premise is refuted only on a reading that the argument does not intend, and I would not defend that reading. The literature on truthmaking as in [W4405407480.c014] concerns multiple truthmakers for one truth, which I grant. It does not show that one existence is wholly self-grounded and also grounded elsewhere. I therefore hold that c009 survives on the aseity reading, but I concede that the premise as worded is ambiguous and needs the qualifier 'wholly' to block the City X counterexample.
turn.revised_premise: It is contradictory for something to exist wholly through itself (in the sense of aseity, with no ground in anything distinct from its own nature) and also through another.

turn.speaker: defender_b
turn.content:
You attribute to the argument an essence-grounding sense of 'through itself' and a sustaining-causal sense of 'through another,' but that is your distinction, not the argument's. The argument does not claim that 'through itself' merely fixes essence while 'through another' sustains existence; it treats 'existing through itself' as absolute aseity in a single order of being, and 'through another' as derivative, dependent being. In the classical framework the argument inhabits, if Ostra depends on a spring for continuance, she simply does not exist through herself at all. Aquinas assumes an identity between essence and existence in God precisely to block any such gap [W2777712853.a1], and he holds that God alone brings about existence absolutely [W3216065113.a1]. Still, your objection lands partly: the premise as stated is an unqualified universal, and your Ostra case shows that cross-categorial combination is possible. To survive, the argument must be revised to say that a thing cannot exist both through itself and through another in the same respect or order of being.

Revised premise: In the same respect or order of being, it is contradictory for something to exist both through itself and through another.

turn.speaker: defender_b
turn.content:
You rightly note that truthmaker theory allows a proposition to have multiple truthmakers without contradiction [W7172336769.c066], and your City X case shows that distinct facts can sustain an entity in different respects. But the argument never intended c009 as a general semantic principle about propositions; it intended it as a metaphysical claim about divine aseity. The fear is that a composite God would depend on distinct properties as final causes or as grounding constituents [W4229080938.c012, W4229080938.arg1.r2]. City X is disanalogous: it is a contingent aggregate, not a necessary being whose existence is identical to its essence, and its charter is an extrinsic legal fact rather than a metaphysical constituent. On a truthmaker view, God Himself grounds divine predicates without property exemplification [W7172336769.c066], because God's being alone metaphysically grounds the truth of such propositions [W7172336769.c072]. Still, your objection shows that c009, as worded, is too broad. The argument survives only if we restrict c009 to the order of constitutive being.

Revised premise: It is contradictory for a being of absolute aseity to exist through itself while also deriving its existence from distinct metaphysical constituents in the same order of being.

objection.text: Consider Maren, a glassblower whose breath is her own: she exists wholly through her own lungs and heart, yet she also owes her existence, continuing each moment, to her parents' original gametes and to the ongoing biosphere that sustains her. Suppose we say she exists 'wholly through herself' in the sense that nothing in her essence is borrowed, and 'through another' in the sense that her causal history and sustenance come from others. Nothing contradictory follows: a thing can have its existence sustained by others while its essence is identical to what it is. Maren's existence is not wholly through herself, since she is dependent, and the revised premise is satisfied only because 'wholly' is read as 'entirely from its own essence.' But the premise needs 'wholly through itself' to exclude 'partly through another.' A being could be wholly self-existent in essence while receiving sustaining activity from another without any incoherence, so the premise's contradiction depends on an equivocation between 'wholly through itself' as essential and as total causal independence.
